name: Carla Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a finish carpenter on new housing estates, what we call second fix. After the walls are plastered I come in and hang the doors, fit skirting boards and window boards, put up the stair rails, sometimes fit kitchens. This month it's a development of sixty family houses on the edge of town, and I'm usually doing four houses a week. I like the bit where a bare shell starts looking like a home somebody will live in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come into the trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Late. I worked in a textile mill until I was thirty, and when it shut I did a one-year carpentry course the council paid for. That course changed my life, so I've got a soft spot for public training. My husband Dev drives city buses, our two boys are grown and gone, and the house is nearly paid off, so we're in a good place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief, and then I'd probably say it's a shame it didn't do more of the boring stuff. At work we'd joke about it at break, like we did with those smart helmets they tried on us that nobody wore. I'm not big online, maybe a comment in the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, and honestly that's fine. I've got about six years to go and they'll go the same as the last ten. I'd have liked it to do our snag lists, though, those are a nightmare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am at Halden Homes. I'd still use the chat thing on my phone now and then, like when I need to write a polite email to the site manager about a missing delivery. Keep saving into the pension and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit disappointed, if I'm truthful, because I was curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a snag list, for someone who's never been on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the list of little faults the buyer or the inspector finds before handover, a door that sticks, a gap in the skirting, a scratch on the window board. It's pages of it and you walk round ticking things off. If a computer could sort that by house and by trade, I'd buy it a coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were curious. Curious about what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether these things are any good, I suppose. My son Arjun works in an office and swears by it, I've only dabbled. If it's just hype, then fine, I didn't waste time learning it.

S0.say: I'd say that's a relief and joke about it at break, like the smart helmets nobody wore. Maybe a comment in the family group chat.
S0.think: Nothing changes for me and that's fine, with six years to go. I'd have liked it to take over the snag lists, though.
S0.do: Carries on at Halden Homes and keeps using a phone chatbot now and then for polite emails to the site manager. Keeps paying into her pension as usual.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small bit of disappointment because she was curious.
S0.quote: If a computer could sort that by house and by trade, I'd buy it a coffee.
S0.fieldNote: Carla treats AI as a possible helper with the dull parts of the job, not a threat, and is slightly let down by a world where it fizzles. Her low-key, practical voice stands out. She already uses a chatbot for small office tasks, so she's not starting from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Next one. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need proper retraining paid for by the public and the big builders, like the course that got me into this trade. I'd say it at union meetings and to anyone who says people should just sort themselves out. I've been the person whose mill shut, so I know what it's like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd probably be okay, second fix is fiddly and every house is a bit different. But it brings back the mill, I'm not going to pretend it doesn't. I remember the week the new looms came and the manager said nobody would lose their job, and a year later we all did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the new tools were actually on site, then learn them once I'd seen them work, I'm not first in line but I'm not last. I'd ask Halden to put me on any course going, and I'd use the AI on my phone more for things like the snag lists and ordering. I'd also join the union's training committee, they've asked me before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a cold little memory in the background. That mill feeling doesn't really leave you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you picture the new tools coming on site, what do you actually see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably laser things that mark out where every door goes, and an app that tells you which house is missing which part. Maybe a machine that cuts all the skirting to length in the yard. That last one I'd be fine with, my wrists would thank it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Halden?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The labourers, the young ones who carry and clean up. If machines move the boards and sweep up, that's the first rung of the ladder gone. That's how I'd have started if I'd been younger, so I'd fight for them.

S1.say: I'd say we need public retraining, paid for partly by the big builders, like the course that got me into carpentry. I know what it's like when your mill shuts.
S1.think: I'd probably be okay, because second fix is fiddly and every house is different. But it brings back the mill and the manager who promised no one would lose their job.
S1.do: Learns new tools once she's seen them work on site and asks Halden for any courses. Uses phone AI more for snag lists and ordering, and joins the union's training committee.
S1.feel: Mostly fine, with a cold memory of the mill closing in the background.
S1.quote: I remember the week the new looms came and the manager said nobody would lose their job, and a year later we all did.
S1.fieldNote: The mill closure is the lens Carla sees all of this through, and it makes her more wary than her secure position would suggest. She wants public training because it once rescued her. Her worry is for labourers at the bottom of the ladder rather than herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the mill all over again, just for everybody at once. I'd say the government has to step in with a proper income for people who lose work and stop the builders from just pocketing the savings. I'd probably even post about it, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Dev and I would be alright for money, we've planned for retirement and we'd just start it early. What frightens me is my boys, both in their thirties, and the whole street. I'd be fine, and everyone around me wouldn't be, and I don't know how you live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd sit down with our pension adviser and see what stopping at sixty looks like. I'd go to the union rallies and sign every petition for a public income, and in the first year after it arrives I'd take early retirement if Halden offered a deal. I'd also put some savings aside in case one of the boys needed help with rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, yes. Not for my own bread, more a weight on my chest for other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your boys would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arjun, the office one. He does insurance claims, and if AI can do almost anything, that's gone in a week. My younger one, Kiran, is a gas engineer, I think he'd have a bit longer, crawling under floors is hard for a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd retire early but also want a public income for others. Would you take that income yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was for everybody, yes, I'm not proud. But I'd want it to go to people who need it before me. We've got the house and the pension, so I'd be at the back of that queue, happily.

S2.say: I'd say it's the mill all over again for everybody at once. Government must step in with an income for those who lose work and stop the builders pocketing the savings.
S2.think: Dev and I would be alright, we'd just start retirement early. What frightens me is my boys and the whole street, being fine while everyone around me isn't.
S2.do: Sees a pension adviser about stopping at sixty and goes to union rallies and petitions for a public income. Takes early retirement if Halden offers a deal and keeps savings ready to help her sons with rent.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a weight on her chest for other people more than for herself.
S2.quote: I'd be fine, and everyone around me wouldn't be, and I don't know how you live with that.
S2.fieldNote: Carla's money keeps her in control, so her anxiety is almost entirely about her sons and neighbours. She is clear she'd stand at the back of the queue for public help. Her politics are personal, built from one course that changed her life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them like they did with the mills. Training now, public jobs, and make the companies pay into it. I'd say it to the union and at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is nearly to the end of my working life anyway. I'd finish my time and step off as it arrives. The thing I'd worry about is Arjun, and I'd nag him to start learning something hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Halden and put extra into savings, maybe an extra few hundred a month, so we could stop at sixty-one without worry. I'd get properly good with the AI on my phone, since if it's coming it's worth knowing. And I'd sit Arjun down and offer to help pay for a course while he still has a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but steady. Like when you know the inspector is coming on Friday, you've got time to fix things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What course would you suggest to Arjun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, maybe the same as mine, or plumbing, something with hands and houses. I don't know if it would last either, nobody does. But it's better than sitting at a desk waiting for the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why learn AI properly yourself if you'll be retiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to understand what's happening to my boys and my street. I learned carpentry at thirty when I didn't think I could. I'm not going to be the mum who doesn't get it.

S3.say: I'd say let's not waste five years like they did with the mills. Training now, public jobs, and make the companies pay into it.
S3.think: Five years is nearly the end of my working life, so I'd step off as it arrives. My worry is Arjun, and I'd nag him to learn something hands-on.
S3.do: Puts a few hundred extra a month into savings to stop at sixty-one and learns AI tools properly. Offers to help her son pay for a hands-on course while he still has a salary.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, like knowing the inspector comes Friday and there's time to fix things.
S3.quote: I'm not going to be the mum who doesn't get it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Carla's timing lines up neatly with her retirement and her focus moves fully to her elder son. She would learn AI not for her job but to understand her family's world. She admits nobody knows which trades would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it right, with free courses and some kind of shared income, and I'd hold the government to it. I'd say it calmly, though, nobody listens to shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it's gone past my working life, I'd be sixty-eight. So it's about the boys and future grandchildren. And maybe I'd volunteer teaching carpentry, if anyone still wants to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire at sixty-four like we planned and keep going until then. Over the decade I'd use the AI tools as they get better and help on the union training committee. After I stop I'd like to volunteer at the community workshop on Mill Lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little sad that the thing that saved me might not save anyone in 2040.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mill Lane, is that near the old mill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's in the old mill, actually, they turned part of it into a community workshop. There's a lovely irony in that. I'd teach people to make a bookshelf in the building where I lost my first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to get right in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Courses that are free and close to home, like mine was. And not making people feel like failures, because when the mill shut some of the men never got over the shame. That's what I'd want them to get right.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time to do it right with free courses and some shared income. I'd hold the government to it, calmly, because nobody listens to shouting.
S4.think: It's past my working life, so it's about the boys and future grandchildren. Maybe I'd volunteer teaching carpentry if anyone still wants to learn.
S4.do: Works on to sixty-four as planned while using AI tools as they improve and helping on the union training committee. Plans to volunteer at the community workshop in the old mill after retiring.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a little sadness that the trade that saved her might not save anyone later.
S4.quote: I'd teach people to make a bookshelf in the building where I lost my first job.
S4.fieldNote: This is the scenario where Carla relaxes, because the change lands after her working life. Her story about the community workshop in the old mill was the most moving moment of the interview. She stresses shame as much as money when talking about job loss.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for me, for Arjun and the young ones on site who haven't built anything up yet. What would help is free courses close to home and a proper income while people retrain, paid for partly by the companies saving money. And someone treating people with respect while it happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people are proud of. I'm proud of a door that closes with a soft click, and nobody asks about that. If the machines take the work, people still need something to be proud of.

headlineQuote: I'm proud of a door that closes with a soft click, and nobody asks about that.
portrait: Carla Gupta is a 58-year-old finish carpenter on new housing estates who came to the trade at thirty after her textile mill shut and a council-paid course rescued her. Married to a bus driver with a nearly paid-off house, she's financially secure and uses a phone chatbot now and then. She's calm if AI fizzles, uneasy in steady change because it brings back the mill, and anxious in the two-year AGI scenario mostly for her sons and neighbours. With more time she plans, saves and nudges her elder son towards a hands-on course. She wants public training and respect for people who lose work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, not for herself but for her son Arjun and young workers who haven't built anything up yet.
whatWouldHelp: Free courses close to home and an income while people retrain, paid for partly by the companies saving money, with people treated with respect.
